- **The dispatch capsule / governance context now renders the same profile-cited directive/tactic (and styleguide/toolguide) sections that `profiles show` does, composing `specializes_from` lineage** (#4917). An agent profile is resolved through two accessors on the same activation-aware `DoctrineService`, and only one composed inheritance: `profiles show` and the runtime bridge read the ungated `agent_profile_repository.resolve_profile()`, which unions a profile's cited references up its `specializes_from` chain, while the dispatch-capsule funnel (`charter/activation/profile_resolution.py`) read the gated `agent_profiles` dict / `repo.get()` — the raw, un-composed record. **Before:** a project- or built-in-layer profile that `specializes_from` an abstract base and cited directives/tactics **only on the ancestor** showed those sections in `profiles show` but silently omitted them from the dispatch capsule — two different governance envelopes for the same profile. **After:** every capsule path (the built-in bootstrap path *and* the activation-aware map — which #4912 now routes all rooted callers through) composes lineage through the same `resolve_profile`, so the two surfaces are byte-identical on the cited sections. The activation semantics are pinned and asserted: lineage composition is **below the activation grain** — the *leaf* profile id is still gated by `activated_agent_profiles` (a de-activated leaf is omitted), but composition may cross into a **de-activated ancestor** (matching the `agent_profile_repository` contract and `profiles show`'s FR-015 behavior), so deactivating an abstract base never strips an activated child of its inherited citations. Composition is best-effort: a broken lineage (missing parent / cycle) falls back to the raw record so the prompt build never collapses. Red-first parity tests pin both funnel paths and the de-activated-ancestor decision. Note: the sibling charter-interview accessor `resolve_governance_for_profile` (`charter/activation/resolver.py`) shares the same root cause on a different surface and is left for a follow-up; builds on #4912/#4838 (the no-org-pack routing landed just ahead of this) in the same family (epic #901).
- **Verdict-recording commands no longer silently drop previously-committed rows from a coordination-resident matrix and exit success** (#4858, #4868, #4884). Three verdict flows shared one defect class — a write that overwrites the whole matrix from a stale, partial, or wrong-source view. **#4858 (concurrency, acceptance matrix):** `acceptance-verdict` read the matrix once, ran its slow negative-invariant check, then wrote the whole in-memory object back with no lock, so two concurrent invocations for *different* entries lost a committed row and the mission's `overall_verdict` flipped `fail → pass` (both still exiting 0) — on flat and coordination layouts. **After:** the mutate→write is a locked read-modify-write — the slow check runs *outside* the lock, then inside `status/locking.py::feature_status_lock` (keyed on the git common dir, so one lock file coordinates the primary checkout and every coordination worktree) the command re-reads the on-disk matrix, splices in *only* the row it owns (a criterion id or invariant id — never resetting a judged negative invariant back to `pending`), and writes+commits, all inside the lock; on a lock-acquisition timeout it fails **closed** (no write, non-zero exit) rather than falling back to an unlocked write; `overall_verdict` is emitted from the re-read+spliced matrix; and the shared `write_acceptance_matrix` now writes through `kernel.atomic.atomic_write` (tempfile + rename), so no reader observes a torn file. **#4868 (serial migration, issue matrix):** on a coordination mission with a legacy `issue-matrix.md` on its authoritative coord branch, `issue-verdict` migrated the *wrong source directory* on the first JSON write (`_migrate_if_needed` passed the primary `feature_dir` to `migrate_issue_matrix_to_json` instead of the coord-aware `read_dir`), so recording a *different* issue produced a canonical JSON containing only that issue and every prior verdict vanished from active state. **After:** `migrate_issue_matrix_to_json` gains an optional `read_dir` and reads the legacy matrix from the authoritative surface, preserving existing rows before upserting the requested issue, while the write still stages on the primary copy so the write-seam's coord materialization and primary-residue cleanup are unchanged; a malformed authoritative matrix now surfaces a structured `IssueVerdictError` instead of silently dropping rows. **#4884 (concurrency, issue matrix):** `issue-verdict` had the same unlocked read-modify-write as #4858 on its sibling artifact — two concurrent invocations for *different* issues each read the whole row set, upserted their own issue, and wrote it back, so the later writer dropped the earlier issue's committed verdict. **After:** the read→upsert→write is the same locked read-modify-write — inside `feature_status_lock` the command re-reads the on-disk issue matrix, splices in only the issue it owns, and writes+commits (fail-closed on lock timeout), with `write_issue_matrix` routed through `kernel.atomic.atomic_write`. All three roots are ATDD red-first (deterministic, no-real-threads reproductions committed before each fix; the #4858/#4884 lock and re-read-inside-lock ordering, the fail-closed-on-timeout behavior, and the #4868 write-staging invariant are each gated by tests — the most dangerous "green but broken" mutants were confirmed to be killed by their guards during review). Uses only the sanctioned `kernel.locks` / `kernel.atomic` primitives; no new `--feature` surface; no `src/specify_cli/__init__.py` change. The P2 restage-clobber neighbour #2482 (same file, different mechanism) is intentionally left out of scope.
- **`spec-kitty init` and the upgrade migrations no longer delete operator-authored commands, skills, command-templates, governance files, or scripts by name — they preserve anything whose package ownership cannot be proven** (#4859, #4861, #4862; closes epic #4792, advances epic #3347). The mutating flows (`init` cleanup and the retirement/rename migrations) removed user-visible assets on directory/basename identity alone: a name match was treated as proof of package ownership, so an operator's hand-authored file that happened to sit at a retired path was destroyed with no backup. **Before:** `init` in global-runtime mode `rmtree`'d `.kittify/command-templates/` (an operator-authorable legacy resolver tier) alongside the package-managed `templates`/`.scratch`; the standalone-skill-surface retirement (#4859) and charter rename (#4862) deleted governance/skill files by name; the python-only migration deleted user `.sh`/`.ps1` scripts. **After:** every such removal routes through the shared `specify_cli.asset_preservation` guard, which PERFORMS the delete only when a content-based prover (manifest `content_hash`, package-managed/regenerable contract, or a `<!-- spec-kitty-command-version:` marker / canonical-byte match) proves ownership; an unprovable collision is preserved in place, or archived verbatim to a timestamped `.kittify/.backup-<ts>/` when its parent is being removed, and surfaced as a warning (never a non-zero exit). Genuinely package-owned targets are still removed and their manifest entries pruned. The data-loss class is closed by construction by a non-vacuous architectural gate (`tests/architectural/test_mutation_ownership_routing.py`, sharing census plumbing with the git-op gate via `_destructive_op_census.py` and proven fail-able by self-mutation in both directions): a routed fix-site carries no raw destructive literal, and any new un-rationalized `rmtree`/`unlink`/`rmdir`/`move` in `init.py` or a migration fails the gate. This is a bug-fix — no CLI version bump.
- **A merge touching a mission's `acceptance-matrix.json` no longer silently flips an accepted verdict to `fail`; a genuine verdict conflict now stops the merge for a human to resolve** (#4880). The row-aware matrix merge driver previously handled a both-sides-diverged field on a keyed row (e.g. `pass_fail`) by embedding a git-style conflict-marker string as the field's own value and letting the merge proceed — for the acceptance matrix, that embedded marker was then read back by the artifact's own verdict computation and recomputed `overall_verdict` to `fail`, silently corrupting an already-accepted mission's recorded state; the issue matrix (which has no computed verdict) instead had the marker string corrupt the affected row's values. The driver now fails closed narrowly: only a genuinely-diverged **verdict** field (two lanes recording *different* authored verdicts, e.g. `pass` vs `fail`) raises and stops the merge for a human. An unset placeholder (`pending`/`unknown`) yields to the authored side, and non-verdict fields prefer the target — so a scaffold row still yields to a filled one and ordinary lane consolidations are unaffected. Non-authoritative prose (the review-cycle `.md`) is unchanged.
- **`spec-kitty upgrade` no longer certifies an interrupted lifecycle-envelope migration as successful, so its own prescribed repair actually works** (#4876; fixes #4872). **Before:** if a lifecycle event log still carried a `.pre-migration.bak` snapshot from an earlier interrupted run, the migration refused that one file but the upgrade still exited 0, printed `✓ migrate_lifecycle_envelope`, stamped the migration `result: success`, and advanced project metadata — leaving the log in its legacy (schema 5) shape. Following the on-screen remedy (remove the stale `.pre-migration.bak`, then rerun `spec-kitty upgrade`) reported the migration "already applied, skipping", so the log stayed legacy forever. **After:** a per-file refusal fails the aggregate migration result, so the runner records it `failed` (never marked applied) and leaves the project's version and schema stamp untouched; every other log in the same walk still migrates. Once the operator removes the stale snapshot, an ordinary `spec-kitty upgrade` retries the failed migration and converges the remaining log. Red-first `@pytest.mark.regression` coverage drives the real migration and the real `MigrationRunner` ledger across the first failed run and the repaired retry.
- **A merged mission whose only completion proof is its `merged_*` markers can now be re-opened, instead of the command failing and then refusing every retry** (#4870). **Before:** `spec-kitty mission reopen` cleared the `merged_*` completion markers from `meta.json` *before* writing the `MissionReopened` audit event. For a "marker-only" mission (completed by merge, with no terminal work packages), clearing first left the canonical event producer's fail-closed completion guard with nothing to prove the mission had completed — so the reopen failed, and because the command had already deleted the sole proof, an unchanged retry was ineligible too: the mission was wedged. **After:** the command snapshots the markers, writes the audited reopen event (carrying that snapshot for reversibility) while the proof is still present, and only then clears the markers — so completion stays provable through the guard, and any refusal before the event is persisted leaves `meta.json` byte-for-byte untouched. The `merged_*` field membership is single-sourced through one `snapshot_merge_metadata` authority shared by the audit payload and the clear. Should the trailing clear itself fail after the event is recorded (deleted/corrupt `meta.json`, I/O error), the command now surfaces a clean, retryable error (`mission_reopen_clear_failed`) — rerunning `reopen` heals it — rather than an unhandled traceback. Red-first CLI coverage drives the real Typer `reopen` command over both independent completion alternatives (marker-only and terminal-WP-only) and the post-emit clear-failure path.
- **`spec-kitty merge --abort` on a mission that has no active merge state no longer fabricates a completion record on the mainline or deletes the mission's live coordination worktree** (#4863). This is the `merge --abort` sibling of the rc4 #4765 `mission close` fix: the same successful-completion path was still reachable through a different live entry point. **Before:** running `merge --abort --mission <slug>` when no Spec Kitty merge state existed treated a merely-resolvable mission handle as proof of an active merge — it printed "No active merge state found … Workspace cleaned up" and exited 0, but on the way it committed a `retrospective.yaml` with `kind: runtime_post_completion` to the target branch, appended a `RetrospectiveCaptured` event, and tore down the coordination worktree of a mission that had never merged. Downstream tooling then counted the in-flight mission as completed, and that premature snapshot could suppress the real retrospective at eventual completion. **After:** the destructive abort path runs only when active merge state exists for the mission. With no state, abort is inert — it may still clean genuinely orphaned merge-runtime scratch, but leaves the target branch, the mission ledger, the retrospective, and the coordination worktree untouched, printing "Coordination workspace left unchanged." A genuine abort still tears down its coordination topology but now bypasses the completion terminus (`persist=False`), so recovery is never stamped with successful-completion provenance. Red-first `@pytest.mark.regression` coverage drives the real `spec-kitty merge --abort` entry point over both the no-state and real-abort cases.
- **The shipped `spec-kitty-mission-review` skill no longer reports a false Gate 3 HARD FAIL for a cross-repo E2E scenario that was deleted upstream** (#5136; resolves #5003, #4949). **Before:** the skill's Step 8.5 Gate 3 floor still listed the retired `saas_sync_enabled.py` scenario (FR-040) alongside the three scenarios that actually exist, and its Gate 1/Gate 3 commands and report template told reviewers to export `SPEC_KITTY_ENABLE_SAAS_SYNC=1` — a flag with no effect, since `tests/contract/` never reads it and none of the surviving E2E scenarios honor the outer shell's value. A reviewer following the skill literally would hit a hard gate failure hunting for a scenario file that no longer exists. **After:** Gate 3's floor is the three surviving scenarios (`dependent_wp_planning_lane.py`, `uninitialized_repo_fail_loud.py`, `contract_drift_caught.py`); the retired scenario, FR-040, and the `SPEC_KITTY_ENABLE_SAAS_SYNC` pin are gone from the skill and from the cross-repo E2E gate runbook it links to (`docs/migrations/cross-repo-e2e-gate.md`), whose worked exception example now uses a placeholder instead of the deleted scenario.
- **Concurrent mission creation within one process — threads calling mission creation from a long-lived host or parallel tooling — could intermittently fail with `TemplateConfigurationError` ("... is missing the requested mapping key") or silently resolve a mission type with a missing step** (#4589). Mission-template resolution shared a single YAML parser and a shared cache-population path across threads, so two threads resolving different mission types could interleave and observe each other's partial state. **After:** resolution is now thread-safe — each thread parses YAML into its own thread-local holder, and cache population is single-flight (one thread populates, the rest wait for its result) — with no change to single-threaded behavior or public APIs.
- **Deleting a lane branch and worktree no longer silently loses its committed work** (#5115). **Before:** for `lanes` missions, re-running `implement` after the lane branch and worktree were deleted quietly started an empty lane and stranded the commits. **After:** `implement` refuses with `DESTROYED_LANE`, names the lost commit, and prints the one-line restore command (`git branch <b> refs/spec-kitty/lane-tip/<b>`). Lanes that were squash-merged can still be reopened; recognising them needs git 2.38 or newer, and older git refuses instead. If spec-kitty never saw the lane's tip, it refuses with `LANE_WORK_TIP_UNKNOWN` and explains how to recover or clean up. It also refuses that way when the lane-tip hook is not active in your repository (for example a husky or other in-tree `core.hooksPath`, or your own `post-commit` hook) and the recorded commit never moved, because spec-kitty cannot tell an empty lane from one whose commits it never saw.
- **Moving a planning work package to review no longer needs `--force`, and review needs real work** (#5100). **Before:** `move-task --to for_review` on a planning-artifact work package looked for a lane worktree that never exists and demanded `--force`. **After:** it passes once the deliverable is committed. For code work packages of a `single_branch` mission, `for_review` is refused until there is a real commit since the claim (claim bookkeeping does not count), and `move-task` never sweeps unrelated uncommitted files into a commit.
